Execration
eks-e-krā'shun
n. (a curse; specifically, a people whose name becomes the form of words others use when cursing)
Latin execratio, from exsecrari, to curse. The Hebrew alah is an oath or curse, and the sense here is technical: to become an execration is to have one's name used as the pattern for a curse.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah warns the remnant against going down to Egypt: “so shall my fury be poured forth upon you, when ye shall enter into Egypt: and ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and ye shall see this place no more” (Jeremiah 42:18). They went, and the sentence was repeated: “they shall even be consumed by the sword and by the famine: they shall die, from the least even unto the greatest… and they shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach” (Jeremiah 44:12). Four nouns describe one fate, and the first is the most chilling. To become an execration is not merely to be cursed but to become the words — the byword others reach for when they wish evil on someone. The people who were called to be a blessing to all the families of the earth end as the standard form of a curse. Jeremiah adds that escape will be almost total in its absence: “none shall return but such as shall escape” (Jeremiah 44:14). The tragedy is that they had asked Jeremiah for the word of the LORD and promised to obey it, and then did the opposite.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines execration as a cursing, a curse pronounced, and imprecation of evil.

expand to see more

EXECRATION, n. The act of cursing; a curse pronounced; imprecation of evil.

EXECRATE, v.t. To curse; to denounce evil against, or to imprecate evil on.

BYWORD, n. A common saying; a proverb; a term of reproach.

REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; abusive language.

ASTONISHMENT, n. Amazement; confusion of mind from fear, surprise or admiration.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 42:18 — "For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; As mine anger and my fury hath been poured forth upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem; so shall my fury be poured forth upon you, when ye shall enter into Egypt: and ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and ye shall see this place no more."

Jeremiah 44:12 — "And I will take the remnant of Judah, that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, and they shall all be consumed, and fall in the land of Egypt; they shall even be consumed by the sword and by the famine: they shall die, from the least even unto the greatest, by the sword and by the famine: and they shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach."

Jeremiah 44:14 — "So that none of the remnant of Judah, which are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall escape or remain, that they should return into the land of Judah, to the which they have a desire to return to dwell there: for none shall return but such as shall escape."

Deuteronomy 25:19 — "Therefore it shall be, when the LORD thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it."

Modern Corruption

Guidance is sought from God with the decision already made, and Jeremiah 42 records what that costs.

expand to see more

The chapter around this word is the most exact account in Scripture of insincere enquiry. The remnant came to Jeremiah, asked him to pray, and swore that whether the answer was good or evil they would obey. They waited ten days for the word. It came, it told them to stay, and they immediately accused Jeremiah of lying and went to Egypt. The pattern is common and it is not confined to nations: guidance is sought after the decision has been taken, and the answer is tested against the decision rather than the decision against the answer. What made their case so grave was the oath. They had bound themselves in advance to obey a word they had not yet heard, and then refused it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is what the sentence actually names. Israel was called in Abraham so that in him all families of the earth should be blessed, and a covenant people who abandon their calling do not become neutral — they become an execration, the form of words others use to curse. That is the trajectory of a church as well as a nation. A congregation exists to be a blessing in its place; when it is not, it does not simply fade quietly but becomes a byword in the community it was sent to serve, and every reader will know an instance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew alah, an oath or curse — Jeremiah 42:18, 44:12; joined with shammah (astonishment), qelalah (a curse) and cherpah (reproach) in the fourfold sentence.

expand to see more

Hebrew alah — an oath, an imprecation; rendered execration in Jeremiah 42:18 and 44:12.

Hebrew shammah — astonishment, horror; the second term of the fourfold sentence.

Hebrew qelalah — a curse; the third, and the counterpart of the blessing promised to Abraham.

Hebrew cherpah — reproach, disgrace; the fourth term.

Jeremiah 42:5-6 records the oath they broke: the LORD be a true and faithful witness between us, whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey.

Usage

"“Ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach”."

"To become an execration is to become the words others curse with."

"They swore to obey the answer before they heard it, and refused it when it came."
